definition: Obdurate means unyielding to persuasion, pity, or moral appeals.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word obdurate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know obdurate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The warden stayed obdurate even after hundreds of letters begged him to reopen the old case.
Firm describes someone who holds a position steadily but can still be reasoned with; obdurate goes further, suggesting a heart hardened against every plea.
Implacable is even stronger than obdurate — an implacable person cannot be appeased at all, ever, while an obdurate one is 'merely' deaf to persuasion and pity.

Unyielding means refusing to give ground under any kind of pressure — force, argument, demands, time. Obdurate is narrower and darker: hardened specifically against appeals to pity, conscience, and persuasion. A cliff face is unyielding; only a heart that hears the plea and still refuses is obdurate.

Hardhearted names a general lack of pity or warmth toward others' suffering — an everyday word for a cold nature. Obdurate is more specific and more literary: appeals have actually been made — tears, arguments, conscience — and every one has bounced off. A hardhearted person may never be tested; an obdurate one refuses appeal after appeal.

Obdurate means unyielding to persuasion, pity, or moral appeals.
For ten years, descendants of the sculptor asked the collector to return the bronze figure to their village square.
Historians wrote open letters, and schoolchildren mailed drawings of the empty pedestal.
The collector read every appeal, admitted the family's grief was real, and refused each request without exception.
Friends said no appeal to conscience had ever moved him on any matter of property.
His heart, one curator sighed, was simply obdurate.
The collector hears every emotional and moral appeal, admits they are moving, and still refuses every single time — that hardened resistance to pity is exactly what obdurate describes.
formal, literary; usually disapproving
Obdurate is the harshest of this unit's 'stubborn' words: it suggests a heart hardened against pity or moral appeals specifically.
Unlike obstinate (a general refusal to change one's mind or course) or adamant (loud, emphatic insistence on a particular point), obdurate implies that even tears and conscience cannot get through.

When the reservoir company announced it would flood the valley, the village tried everything short of the courts.
Letters came first, then a delegation of farmers, then the schoolchildren's choir singing on the company's marble steps.
Through it all the chairman remained obdurate: he received each group courteously, heard the pleas to the end, and refused every one without the smallest change in terms.
Even his own engineers proposed a compromise line that would spare the church and half the orchards; he dismissed it the same afternoon.
Villagers said afterward that arguing with him was like knocking on a sealed door — the knock was always answered, and the door never opened.
